The classification is derived from the graph structure, not authored. Stored classification metadata must agree with the derived one.

docs.title: Cluster goal
docs.text:
DE: Cluster-Ziel — see Graph Definition

A goal with at least one contains child. Clusters serve navigation, filtering, and aggregated progress. Their satisfaction is derived from their atomic descendants rather than recorded directly.

docs.title: Atomic basis
docs.text:
DE: atomare Basis — see Graph Definition

Written \(\mathrm{Atoms}(g)\): the goal itself if it is atomic, otherwise its atomic contains descendants. It is the set whose mastery witnesses satisfaction of a cluster.

docs.title: contains
docs.text:
DE: enthält — see Graph Definition

The authored hierarchy relation \(C\): \((p, c)\) means parent \(p\) directly contains child \(c\) in content terms. Its arrow points from parent to child. contains must be acyclic but allows multiple parents (polyhierarchy).

Ancestor/descendant relationships are derived through paths of one or more contains edges. contains is not a prerequisite and not a program placement.

docs.title: requires
docs.text:
DE: setzt voraus — see Graph Definition

The authored prerequisite relation \(R\): \((g, p)\) means goal \(g\) directly requires prerequisite \(p\). Its arrow points from the dependent goal to its prerequisite; \(p\) must be satisfied before \(g\) is approached. It must be acyclic. Under the binding target state, all authored requires edges connect atomic goals (\(R \subseteq A \times A\)); existing prerequisites on clusters are evaluated via contains inheritance and atomic expansion during migration.

Both contains and requires record direct relationships; derived relationships are computed rather than modeled as extra relation types.

docs.title: Inherited prerequisites
docs.text:
DE: vererbte Voraussetzungen — see Graph Definition

Additional prerequisites derived from the requires of a goal's contains ancestors, excluding pairs already authored on the goal itself: \(R_{\mathrm{inherited}} = R_{\mathrm{eff}} \setminus R\). With multiple parents, all ancestor paths contribute. Inheritance through containment is distinct from following a chain of prerequisites.

docs.title: Effective prerequisites
docs.text:
DE: effektive Voraussetzungen — see Graph Definition

The derived prerequisite relation \(R_{\mathrm{eff}} = R \cup R_{\mathrm{inherited}}\), combining a goal's own requires with prerequisites inherited from its contains ancestors and expanded onto atomic basis goals (\(R_{\mathrm{at}}\)). In a fully atomic-authored prerequisite graph, authored and effective atomic prerequisites coincide.

docs.title: Prerequisite reachability
docs.text:
DE: Erreichbarkeit von Voraussetzungen — see Graph Definition

Goals connected by one or more edges of the specified prerequisite relation, written \(R^+\) or \(R_{\mathrm{at}}^+\). This transitive closure includes single edges and longer chains. A learning-flow view uses the inverse direction and labels it explicitly.

docs.title: Weight
docs.text:
DE: Gewicht — see Graph Definition and AGENTS.md

A strictly positive number expressing a goal's share in progress. Convention in the canonical landscapes: atomic goals carry weight = 1, clusters carry the number of their unique atomic descendants, so a goal reachable through several parents is counted once.

docs.title: Goal ID and shortKey
docs.text:
DE: Lernziel-ID, Kurzschlüssel — see Graph Definition

id is the canonical UUID identity of a goal; it may be shown to learners and coaches and is not an access credential. shortKey is an optional stable ASCII identifier for exports, APIs, and cross-layer references; it is unique per logical landscape and never replaces id.

docs.title: Graph validity
docs.text:
DE: Graphgültigkeit — see Graph Definition

A graph is valid iff IDs are unique, contains, requires, and the effective atomic prerequisite relation are acyclic, and both minimality rules hold:

  • Local minimality: a prerequisite already inherited from a contains ancestor must not be restated on the child node.
  • Transitive minimality: an edge must not be present if the same prerequisite already follows from other effective prerequisite paths.

docs.title: Motivation anchor
docs.text:
DE: Motivationsanker — see Context & Views

An atomic orientation goal that opens a didactic route by answering "why this subject or topic?", for example Warum Physik? – Weltverständnis & Zukunft. Route checks measure connectivity back to such an anchor.

docs.title: Terminal autonomy goal
docs.text:
DE: terminales Autonomieziel — see Context & Views

An atomic goal at which the learner performs independently, typically an exam-mode exercise goal such as the atomic tasks under Übungen Q2. It closes a didactic route.

docs.title: Route coverage
docs.text:
DE: Routenabdeckung — see Context & Views

The property that every route-relevant atomic goal lies on at least one prerequisite path from a motivation anchor to a terminal autonomy goal. The intended learning direction runs from orientation through understanding (and parallel memorization where needed) to independent application.

docs.title: 3. Node types (learning modes)
docs.text: Pedagogical goal kinds are orthogonal to the structural atomic/cluster split. See Node Types.

docs.title: Understanding
docs.text:
DE: Verstehen

The default type: conceptual or procedural competence, coached and practised in dialogue. A goal with no special exam or memorization fields is an Understanding node; orientation goals are marked explicitly and do not test subject knowledge.

docs.title: Memorize
docs.text:
DE: Sich merken

A spaced-repetition goal for facts, vocabulary, notation, or selected formulas. It is mastered only when no required card is due and every required card has passed an unaided verified recall test.

docs.title: Exam
docs.text:
DE: Selbstständig Probleme lösen, Prüfungsknoten

A goal carrying examData: an independent assessment or practice task with a model solution and scoring scheme. requires gates access to the task and drives targeted remediation after an unsuccessful attempt.

docs.title: examData and scoring
docs.text:
DE: Prüfungsdaten, Bewertung — see Node Types

Task content, solution content, and a scoring object with maxPoints, passingPoints, and per-step points: \(\mathrm{total} = \min(\sum \text{step points}, \mathrm{maxPoints})\), passed iff \(\mathrm{total} \ge \mathrm{passingPoints}\). Only passing writes mastery (1.0); an unsuccessful attempt is explained in dialogue without altering stored learner state, so the task can be retried.

docs.title: Exam Mode
docs.text:
DE: Prüfungsmodus — see Node Types

The runtime mode in which the AI coach acts as a strict, neutral exam supervisor: the task is delivered verbatim, no hints are given during work, one complete submission is graded step by step, and only afterwards does the coaching role resume.

docs.title: SRS and SM-2
docs.text:
DE: Kartei, Wiederholungsplanung — see Node Types

Spaced-repetition scheduling following the SuperMemo-2 algorithm. Each card stores interval, repetition, easiness factor ef, and nextReview. A card is due when nextReview <= now or when it has no state yet.

docs.title: Verified recall
docs.text:
DE: geprüfter Abruf — see Node Types

The hard recall gate on memorization cards: the coach shows only the prompt, the learner answers unaided, and only afterwards does the coach retrieve the expected answer and persist passed or failed. Ordinary SRS practice in the Cockpit never substitutes for this check.

docs.title: Layer model
docs.text:
DE: Schichtenmodell — see General Goal System and Migration

SkillPilot separates five layers that older legacy graphs sometimes mixed:

Layer Holds Example Goal layer assessable competences and content clusters "lineare Funktionen verknüpfen" Program layer structural units and learning units Jahrgang 8, E-Phase, module, track, exam, learning unit Placement layer links from goals into program units, including learning-unit ownership "this goal belongs to Q1" Competency-axis layer taxonomy entries K1 Mathematisch argumentieren Composition-view layer scope-specific learner-facing trees DE-BY / Gymnasium / SekII / Mathematik / LK

docs.title: Program unit
docs.text:
DE: Programmeinheit — see View Projection and Goal Placement

An explicit structural container (year, semester, module, phase, track, exam section) forming an ordered tree via parentUnitId and order. A content goal must never be reused as a stand-in for a program unit. A programUnits entry of kind learningUnit declares a learning unit instead of a structural container (see below).

docs.title: Learning unit
docs.text:
DE: Lerneinheit — see Learning Units and Optional Planning (§12)

A recursively composed educational whole with a stated learning outcome, motivational introduction, constituent goals or subunits, and a reviewed completion rule (LearningUnit). A year, semester, or arbitrary navigation cluster does not become a learning unit solely by grouping goals. Since the Product Owner decision of 12 November 2026, a learning unit is declared in the placement layer as a programUnits entry of kind learningUnit with learning promise and revision; it owns atomic goals through goalPlacements of relation own and names the unit that requires it as a child through parentUnitId (field reference).

Each target has one direct acquisition owner in the resolved unit hierarchy; parent units aggregate descendants. Completion follows from required children and the unit's own goal-type obligations without a stored unit-mastery result. An open parent exam does not reopen completed child competencies, and passing a parent exam never passes protected child exams or cards. Effective competence remains global, and individual recognition can precede complete unit completion; it is only sound inside units that satisfy the validity rules R1–R5 of 11 November 2026 (Graph Definition §13.3). This revised concept is not yet implemented in the runtime; see also Learning Unit Progression.

docs.title: Goal placement
docs.text:
DE: Zielplatzierung — see View Projection and Goal Placement

An entry attaching an unchanged goal to a program unit under a reviewed context (primary, secondary, assessed). A placement never re-parents the content contains tree and never creates a duplicate occurrence in the default tree. Relation own records, without context, that a learning unit directly owns an atomic goal; it attaches nothing to the program tree.

docs.title: Competency axis
docs.text:
DE: Kompetenzachse — see View Projection and Goal Placement

An orthogonal taxonomy view built from competencyCatalog plus competencyRefs, for example process competencies K1–K6. Broad capability families are taxonomy entries, neither goals nor program units.

docs.title: Composition view
docs.text:
DE: Composition View, Sichtkomposition — see View Projection and Goal Placement

An explicit, reviewed definition of the learner-facing upper tree for one resolved scope: structure nodes, labels, ordering, and references to canonical subtree roots. It contains neither newly authored atomic goals nor new requires edges and—where present—is the authoritative source for that scope's default tree.

docs.title: Canonical subtree reference
docs.text:
DE: kanonische Teilbaumreferenz — see View Projection and Goal Placement

A pointer from a composition view to a reviewed cluster root of the canonical graph; the subtree contents stay in the canonical model. Within one compiled view tree, expanded references must be pairwise disjoint.

docs.title: Projection role
docs.text:
DE: Projektionsrolle — see View Projection and Goal Placement

Authored per composition-view reference as projectionRole (defaulting to target):

  • target — a selectable learning target in this scope; counts toward navigation, frontier, progress, and completion.
  • prerequisiteOnly — a supporting goal whose global mastery may unlock or block targets but which is not itself selectable here.

Roles are never inferred implicitly from requires, phase, year, or stage. On overlap, specificity decides (direct goalEntry beats subtree role, deeper subtree beats broader subtree; only at equal specificity does target win).

docs.title: Applicability
docs.text:
DE: Gültigkeit, Anwendbarkeit — see Node Types and Context & Views

Optional compiled goal metadata mapping filter dimensions (jurisdiction, schoolForm, stage, durationModel, courseProfile, …) to allowed values. An omitted dimension is unrestricted. Applicability is not a node type and never creates parent edges; it only filters visibility in scoped views.

docs.title: Applicability override
docs.text:
DE: Gültigkeits-Override — see Context & Views

Audit metadata under extendedData.applicabilityOverrides recording which active applicability values were added via an explicit, justified exception rather than ordinary source alignment. At runtime, compiled applicability remains authoritative.

docs.title: Entry scope
docs.text:
DE: Einstiegskontext — see General Goal System and Migration

The small set of contextual choices made before navigating content: school form, stage, jurisdiction, duration model, course profile, current year or phase. Entry scope acts as a query and navigation filter and never forces goal duplication.

docs.title: Resolved scope
docs.text:
DE: aufgelöster Kontext — see View Projection and Goal Placement

A fully determined combination such as DE-HE / Gymnasium / SekII / Mathematik / LK. Default trees, single-occurrence validity, and coverage checks are always evaluated relative to one resolved scope.

docs.title: Default tree
docs.text:
DE: Standardbaum — see View Projection and Goal Placement

The single tree a learner sees for a resolved scope. Every visible edge comes from exactly one explicit source (contains, parentUnitId, goalPlacements, or competencyRefs), never from title or phase heuristics. Single-occurrence rule: within one resolved scope each visible goal appears at most once and under at most one visible parent.

docs.title: Content tree, program tree, competency view
docs.text:
DE: Inhaltsbaum, Programmbaum, Kompetenzsicht — see View Projection and Goal Placement

The three classic view families, each with one structural source of truth (contains for content, programUnits + goalPlacements for program, competencyCatalog + competencyRefs for competency axes), complemented by the scope-specific composition view as the preferred learner-facing default.

docs.title: phase
docs.text:
DE: Phase — see Graph Definition

Compatibility metadata (E, Q1–Q4, …) used for badges, filtering, or migration tooling. phase is explicitly not canonical graph semantics and never implies parentage.

docs.title: ALL
docs.text:
DE: ALL-Platzhalter — see Context & Views

A query-only sentinel meaning "do not restrict this dimension" during scope resolution. ALL must never be serialized as an applicability or placement value.

docs.title: Levels of personalization
docs.text:
DE: Personalisierungsstufen — see Levels of Personalization

The four-step narrowing from curriculum to individual mastery: 1 base curriculum → 2 committed personal curriculum → 3a current focus plus 3b one active atomic goal → 4 global mastery. Catalog navigation such as school, university, or languages precedes Level 1 and is not learner scope.

docs.title: Base curriculum
docs.text:
DE: Basiscurriculum — see Learning Workflow

The skill landscape chosen before learning starts; it provides the full goal universe for that learner.

docs.title: Personal curriculum
docs.text:
DE: persönliches Curriculum, persönlicher Lehrplan — see Learning Workflow

The committed, longer-lived subset of the base curriculum in scope for one learner (jurisdiction or canonical view, applicable duration model, stage, subjects, and course profiles per subject). It resolves the learner-facing composition view and becomes the candidate space for focus, frontier, progress, and completion, while the backend may still consult the full graph for strict prerequisite checks.

This state is backend-owned and configured exclusively through the first-party WebGUI and Cockpit; the chat coach neither asks for nor mutates it.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
DE: Personalisierung — see Behavioral Integration of the MCP Coach

The learner's authored validity choices such as jurisdiction or course profile. Personalization is never inferred from contains or requires. Selectable options always come from the latest backend state as opaque IDs. Course profiles apply per subject so Mathematik LK and Physik GK can coexist.

docs.title: Learning scope and focus
docs.text:
DE: Lernumfang und Fokus — see Behavioral Integration of the MCP Coach

Two levels the coach must keep apart:

  • Learning scope: the committed Personal Curriculum for this learner.
  • Focus (Level 3a): the currently selected subtree or learning corridor (plannedGoals) from which frontier and goal options are drawn. Once the Personal Curriculum is complete, focus is never empty: without a valid explicit selection, the highest first visible root is chosen deterministically. A year or phase may bound focus without becoming a goal.

Frontier and goal recommendations are offered only once scope and focus are resolved.

docs.title: Active goal
docs.text:
DE: aktives Ziel — see Learning Workflow

Exactly one backend-confirmed atomic goal (Level 3b) currently worked on in UI and coach. Normally drawn from the frontier; for a non-frontier selection, the system diagnoses missing prerequisites rather than silently bypassing them.

docs.title: Frontier
docs.text:
DE: Frontier, nächste erreichbare Lernziele — see Graph Definition

The set of not-yet-mastered atomic goals whose effective prerequisites are all satisfied — the didactic zone of proximal development, deterministically computed from the graph rather than guessed by the AI.

docs.title: Satisfaction
docs.text:
DE: Erfüllung — see Graph Definition

\(\mathrm{Sat}(g)\) holds iff the atomic basis of \(g\) is non-empty and fully mastered. An atomic goal is satisfied iff it is mastered; a cluster iff all its atomic descendants are mastered.

docs.title: Optimistic mode
docs.text:
DE: optimistischer Modus — see Context & Views

Filter to the selected view scope first (including explicit prerequisiteOnly foundations), then evaluate prerequisites. Learners can start directly in their chosen scope without being globally blocked by gaps from earlier years. This is the default mode.

docs.title: Strict mode (pessimistic mode)
docs.text:
DE: strikter Modus, pessimistischer Modus — see Context & Views

Candidates still come from the filtered scope, but prerequisites are enforced globally across the entire graph. Used diagnostically to surface missing foundations outside the active filter (strictMode).

docs.title: Missing prerequisites
docs.text:
DE: fehlende Voraussetzungen — see Context & Views

The unsatisfied effective prerequisites of a goal, split into gaps inside and outside the active filter — the diagnostic answer to "why is this goal still locked?".

docs.title: Mastery
docs.text:
DE: Beherrschung; Lernziel geschafft oder noch nicht geschafft — see Learning Workflow and Implicit Mastery

The single stored outcome for an atomic goal: mastered or not mastered (encodable as 0 and 1, without intermediate partial grades or extra qualification tiers). Mastery belongs to stable goal IDs and applies globally across composition views. Cluster or subject progress is the weighted share of unique mastered atomic goals.

The binding 4 November 2026 concept adds effective mastery \(M_{\mathrm{eff}} = M \cup I\), where \(I\) is derived recognition of ordinary competencies through independent application in valid local assessment contracts. Exam and memory goals never enter \(I\). Runtime adaptation to this extended contract remains pending.

docs.title: Curriculum timeline and pacing plan
docs.text:
DE: Curriculum-Zeitachse, Curriculum-Zeitplan, Stoffverteilungsplan — see Curriculum Timeline, Buffer Planning, and Target-vs-Actual Pacing

A versioned execution-plan overlay assigning resolved curriculum clusters to concrete local date ranges and teaching capacity for a class or learner. It owns calendar, buffer, plan blocks, and revisions without ever writing dates into canonical goals, program units, placements, or composition views.

docs.title: Planning unit
docs.text:
DE: Planungseinheit — see Curriculum Timeline, Buffer Planning, and Target-vs-Actual Pacing

A plan-local unit used to distribute expected curriculum progress across available time capacity (transparent baseline: one unit per schedulable atomic target). It is neither a grade nor canonical weight; baseline mastery before plan start does not count as newly learned planning units.

docs.title: Plan milestone
docs.text:
DE: Planmeilenstein, konkretes Ziel bis Datum — see Curriculum Timeline, Buffer Planning, and Target-vs-Actual Pacing

A dated commitment such as "complete the selected Mathematics Abitur tasks by 15 March". It separates subject-matter kind from deadline rigidity and scheduled workload from mastery-derived completion, driving dated goal lists, forecasts, and replanning without creating mastery on its own.

docs.title: Course plan status snapshot
docs.text:
DE: Kurs-Planlage, Plan-und-Planlage-Seite — see Curriculum Timeline, Buffer Planning, and Target-vs-Actual Pacing

A digest-bound as-of read model of one plan revision showing textual course plan, planned block progress, confirmed teaching coverage, and separately labeled mastery distribution with input-data quality. It introduces no new source of truth alongside plan and mastery data.

docs.title: Learning velocity
docs.text:
DE: Lerngeschwindigkeit — see Learning Velocity

The observed rate of atomic goals becoming mastered over time. The Cockpit chart counts recorded completions per calendar week; a bound pacing plan compares newly achieved planning units per effective teaching week against its target curve. Neither form is a grade or learner ranking.

docs.title: Autopilot
docs.text:
DE: Autopilot — see Frontier Goal Selection Strategies & Autopilot

An opt-in mode that automatically activates the first entry of the strategy-ordered next-steps list once the active goal reaches mastered state.

docs.title: Selection strategy
docs.text:
DE: Auswahlpriorisierung — see Frontier Goal Selection Strategies & Autopilot

How frontier goals are ordered: Random for variety across topic areas, Sequential for linear progression along the curriculum structure. Stored per learner alongside autopilot and strictMode.

docs.title: SkillPilot ID
docs.text:
DE: SkillPilot-ID — see Quickstart

The learner's permanent, pseudonymous key to their learning profile — requiring no registration with name or email address. The permanent SkillPilot ID stays strictly backend-only and never appears as a tool argument, tool result, or chat content.

docs.title: Learning session
docs.text:
DE: Lernsession — see OAuth and Learner Session Architecture

An opaque, randomly generated key with an absolute 24-hour lifetime addressing the exact learner context confirmed by Start learning (Lernen starten). Every start creates a fresh session; the adapter passes it unchanged on every learner-specific tool call.

docs.title: OAuth app binding
docs.text:
DE: OAuth-Verbindung — see OpenAI MCP Client Binding

The revocable OAuth authorization authenticating an approved provider integration against the backend. It authenticates the integration, not the learner: OAuth alone neither selects a learner profile nor creates a learning session.

docs.title: SkillPilot Lerncoach
docs.text:
DE: SkillPilot Lerncoach — see ChatClient/Backend Communication Contract

The AI-facing dialogue layer turning backend state into a learning conversation. The coach leads the dialogue; the backend decides authoritatively on learning state, active filters, allowed transitions, and reachable next steps.

docs.title: Cockpit
docs.text:
DE: Cockpit — see Quickstart

The SkillPilot web surface displaying learning map, progress, learning-plan status, and SRS flashcard practice. Cockpit and coach operate on the same backend learning state; the unaided recall test (Verified Recall) is graded through the coach flow rather than the Cockpit drill.

docs.title: Safe state projection
docs.text:
DE: sichere Zustandsprojektion — see ChatClient/Backend Communication Contract

The rule that only an explicitly allowlisted, data-minimized projection of learner state crosses the provider boundary. Internal identities, secrets, and private file paths are stripped before anything reaches model, chat, or widget.

docs.title: Provider-neutral boundary
docs.text:
DE: providerneutrale Grenze — see ChatClient/Backend Communication Contract

The strict separation between the shared SkillPilot domain core and provider-specific adapters. Domain rules, exam authorization, and state projection live in the shared core so adding or replacing an AI provider never forks learning logic.

docs.title: Curriculum Champion
docs.text:
DE: Curriculum-Champion — see Champion Guide

A subject specialist taking responsibility for the practical trial of a curriculum or a clearly scoped topic area: working through goals as a learner, reporting stumbling blocks directly on the goal or via GitHub, and supporting subject-matter refinement.

docs.title: Four-level champion model
docs.text:
DE: Vier-Stufen-Champion-Modell — see Four-Level Champion Model

The QA cascade separating machine verification from human trials: 1a the automated CI pipeline (active today), 1b static AI review agent and 1c dynamic AI agent, and 2 independent human Champion trials.

docs.title: QA scope
docs.text:
DE: QA-Scope — see Curriculum Quality

An explicitly configured check profile covering one learner-facing curriculum section, defined by curriculum, label (such as Sekundarstufe I), motivation anchors, selected atomic goals, terminal autonomy areas, and cluster selector. A QA scope counts registered check profiles — neither paths in the graph nor exercise counts. The earlier label "Routen" has been retired.

docs.title: CQR rule
docs.text:
DE: CQR-Regel — see Curriculum Quality

A Curriculum-Quality-Review rule with a stable ID evaluated by the quality dashboard, for example CQR-003 for bidirectional jurisdiction coverage or CQR-101 for closed routes. CQR rules judge curriculum content quality.

docs.title: GVR rule
docs.text:
DE: GVR-Regel — see Graph Validation Rules

A Graph-Validation-Rollout rule with a stable ID enforced by the CI validator, for example GVR-001 (no goal may require its own contains ancestor). GVR rules enforce structural graph integrity.

docs.title: Maturity level
docs.text:
DE: Reifegrad — see Curriculum Quality and Quality and Human-Trial Concept

A cumulative, conservative rating (M0–M7) bound to an explicitly named scope and content revision. A single QA scope reaches at most M3; a curriculum can reach M0 through M7. M5 marks core automated readiness (sources captured, jurisdiction views proven bidirectionally, mandatory QA scopes route- and exam-complete). M6 adds the reviewed memory layer; M7 is the fully completed machine QA level across all five per-goal gates (D descriptions, P understanding profiles, A atomicity, M memory, V visualizations).

Human trials by Curriculum Champions are reported as a separate attribute (not M8); M7 alone does not certify human approval or classroom effectiveness.

docs.title: Semantic atomicity
docs.text:
DE: semantische Atomarität — see Semantic Atomicity Review

The subject-matter review question of whether a learning goal truly expresses a single assessable competence rather than bundling multiple skills. Structural atomicity (no contains children) is necessary but not sufficient.

docs.title: Generated artifact
docs.text:
DE: generiertes Artefakt — see Documentation Guidelines

A report, status snapshot, or documentation output produced by a script and carrying an explicit notice naming its generator, regeneration command, and source of truth. Substantive decisions belong in the canonical source files, never as manual edits to the generated artifact.

docs.title: 8. Distinctions that are easy to get wrong
docs.text: These are not the same Why it matters contains vs requires Containment bundles content hierarchically; requires sequences prerequisites. Only requires drives the frontier. contains vs goalPlacement Content composition vs program membership. A placement never re-parents the content tree. requires vs effective prerequisites requires records direct edges; effective prerequisites also include prerequisites inherited from ancestors during migration. Atomic goal vs cluster goal Mastery, frontier, and coverage counts are defined on atomic goals; clusters only aggregate. Structural vs semantic atomicity A leaf node without contains children can still bundle multiple competences. applicability vs projectionRole applicability decides whether a goal is visible in a scope; projectionRole decides whether it is a target or prerequisiteOnly. applicability vs node type applicability is contextual view metadata, not a fourth learning mode. Entry scope vs personal curriculum Entry scope narrows a query; the personal curriculum is the learner's durably committed scope. Learning scope vs focus Scope defines what is relevant overall; focus selects the active working corridor. Frontier vs recommendation The frontier is computed mathematically from graph and mastery; selection strategy and autopilot only order within it. Optimistic vs strict mode Same candidate goals, different prerequisite reach — strict mode is a diagnostic, not a stricter curriculum. SRS practice vs verified recall Practice schedules review intervals; only the unaided coach recall check closes a memorization goal. SkillPilot ID vs learning session Permanent backend-only pseudonymous identity vs fresh 24-hour key sent to the provider integration. OAuth binding vs learning session OAuth authenticates the app/integration; the learning session selects the learner context. phase vs program unit phase is compatibility metadata; only an explicit program unit forms a structural node. Learning unit vs personalization level A recursively composed educational whole with derived completion vs one of the four scope/state layers. Learning unit vs goal difficulty A unit of acquisition and completion vs the demand level of one goal (level). Unit completion vs goal availability Fulfilled child and own obligations vs prerequisites for starting work; a technical whole-unit gate requires a separate policy. QA scope vs learning route A QA scope is a registered check profile, not a single path walked by a learner. CQR vs GVR rules Content quality review vs structural graph validation. Curriculum vs skill graph Normative external document vs versioned operative graph model derived from it. Skill graph vs skill landscape Formal model and semantics vs one delimited, published subject instance with landscapeId, Champion, and maturity level.

docs.title: 1. Ebenen der Personalisierung
docs.text:
Dieses Kapitel beschreibt, wie SkillPilot vom veröffentlichten Curriculum-Katalog bis zur individuellen atomaren Beherrschung eingrenzt. Die vorgeschaltete Katalognavigation liegt vor den vier Personalisierungsebenen und wird niemals als Lernendenzustand gespeichert.

Diese vier Ebenen sind strikt von Lerneinheiten (LearningUnit) zu unterscheiden — rekursiv zusammengesetzten didaktischen Einheiten mit Lernversprechen und abgeleitetem Abschluss, deren Verortung zum aufgelösten Bildungskontext gehört und keine fünfte Personalisierungsebene bildet.

docs.title: 1.1. Vor Ebene 1: Katalognavigation
docs.text: Lernende wählen zunächst einen Katalogbereich wie Schule, Hochschule oder Sprachen und Weiterbildung, um ein passendes Wurzel-Curriculum zu finden. Dieser Schritt dient ausschließlich der Orientierung im Katalog.

docs.title: 1.2. Ebene 1: Basis-Curriculum
docs.text:
Gewählt wird genau ein veröffentlichtes Wurzel-Curriculum, das den vollständigen Zielraum bereitstellt, ohne kanonische Lernziele zu kopieren oder umzubenennen (z. B. Gymnasium (DE), ein Studiengangskatalog oder eine CEFR-Sprach-Skill-Landschaft).

Nur in curricula/curriculum_manifest.json deklarierte Wurzel-Curricula sind in der Oberfläche wählbar und für Champion-Registrierungen zulässig:

{
  "curricula": [
    { "id": "a0e13c56-c25f-4742-9272-3a1a603ee52e", "title": "Gymnasium (DE)" }
  ]
}

Jede Manifest-ID muss unter curricula/ existieren, darf keine Teil- oder Modullandschaft sein und wird in CI gegen die berechnete Wurzelmenge geprüft.

docs.title: 1.3. Ebene 2: Persönlicher Lehrplan (Personal Curriculum)
docs.text:
Der Persönliche Lehrplan ist der verbindliche, längerfristige Lernumfang innerhalb des Basis-Curriculums — er bestimmt die geltende curriculare Sicht und nicht den kurzfristigen Arbeitsfokus. Für deutsche Schulcurricula gilt die semantische Reihenfolge:

  1. Bundesland / Jurisdiktion (einschließlich expliziter kanonischer Sicht, sofern verfügbar);
  2. Dauermodell (z. B. G8 oder G9, sofern landesspezifisch relevant);
  3. Stufe (Sekundarstufe I, Sekundarstufe II oder ausdrücklich beide);
  4. Ausgewählte Fächer;
  5. Kursprofil je gewähltem Fach (sofern einschlägig).

Das Kursprofil hängt am einzelnen Fach: Mathematik LK und Physik GK können parallel gelten, LK impliziert niemals automatisch Sekundarstufe II, und eine fehlende Stufenangabe wird niemals stillschweigend stufenübergreifend gedeutet. Ebene 2 löst die geltende Kompositionsansicht auf und begrenzt Fokus, Frontier, Fortschritt und Abschluss; Änderungen revalidieren Fokus und activeGoal, ohne stabile Ziel-IDs oder globale Mastery zu löschen.

Einheitlicher First-Party-Editorvertrag: Ebene 2 wird ausschließlich im First-Party-WebGUI von SkillPilot gepflegt (vor dem Lernstart auf dem Startbildschirm sowie später im Cockpit) über gemeinsame Backend-Optionen, Validierung und Speicherung. Der OpenAI-ChatClient fragt Ebene 2 weder ab noch verändert er sie; ist sie unvollständig, stoppt er das Fachcoaching und verweist auf das WebGUI.

docs.title: 1.4. Ebene 3: Lernfokus und aktives Lernziel
docs.text:
Ebene 3 ist bewusst leichtgewichtig veränderbar und besteht aus zwei Teilen:

  • Ebene 3a — Fokus: eine oder mehrere Fokuswurzeln, die den aktuellen Lernkorridor wählen (z. B. Jahrgangsstufe 7, Q1 oder Analysis; Programmeinheiten sind selbst keine kanonischen Lernziele).
  • Ebene 3b — Aktives atomares Ziel: höchstens ein konkretes, überprüfbares atomares Lernziel als unmittelbares Arbeitsziel.

Bei einer Fokusweitung veröffentlicht das Backend entlang des sichtbaren Vorfahrenpfads zur Wurzel nur gültige breitere Vorfahren, die noch offene target-Ziele ergänzen (nächstgelegener Vorfahr zuerst, unter Erhalt unabhängiger Mehrfachwurzeln in goalIds). Ein automatischer Vorschlag erfolgt nur nach tatsächlichem Abschluss des aktuellen Fokus (nicht bei bloß blockierter Frontier) und erfordert die Zustimmung der lernenden Person.

Nach der Korrektur vom 4. November 2026 (Abschlusskonzept) schreibt requires allein keine Voraussetzungs-Mastery; bestandene Anwendungsprüfungen begründen global wirksame Anerkennung gewöhnlicher Ziele, die beim Fokusweiten bestehen bleibt.

docs.title: 1.5. Ebene 4: Mastery und orthogonale Zeitachse
docs.text:
Mastery ist das einzige dauerhafte Ergebnis je stabiler atomarer Ziel-UUID — gemeistert oder nicht gemeistert — und gilt global über Kompositionsansichten sowie Ebene-2/3-Wechsel hinweg ohne Teilbeherrschungsstufen. Effektive Beherrschung \(M_{\mathrm{eff}} = M \cup W\) vereint gespeicherte explizite Mastery \(M\) und prüfungsbasierte Anerkennung \(W\) (Prüfungs- und Lernkartenziele bleiben explizit; Laufzeitmigration offen, siehe 2.4). Prozentwerte auf Clustern bezeichnen den gewichteten Anteil effektiv beherrschter Atomziele, niemals Teilmastery eines Einzelziels.

Orthogonale Zeitachse: Ein datierter Kurs- oder Klausurplan ist kein fünftes Personalisierungslevel, sondern eine Ausführungsplanung für das Wann innerhalb von Ebene 2 (siehe Einheitlicher Lernplanstatus und Zeitachsenkonzept).

docs.title: 1. Levels of Personalization
docs.text:
This chapter specifies how SkillPilot narrows from the published curriculum catalog down to individual atomic mastery. Catalog navigation precedes the four personalization levels and is never persisted as learner scope.

These four levels remain distinct from Learning Units (Lerneinheiten, LearningUnit) — recursively composed didactic units with intended outcomes and derived completion whose placement belongs to the resolved educational context rather than forming a fifth personalization level.

docs.title: 1.1. Before Level 1: catalog navigation
docs.text: Learners first choose a catalog area such as school, university and higher education, or languages and continuing education to locate an appropriate root curriculum. This step aids discovery only and stores nothing on the learner record.

docs.title: 1.2. Level 1: Base Curriculum
docs.text:
The learner selects one published root curriculum providing the complete goal universe from which subsequent levels narrow without copying or altering canonical goals (for example Gymnasium (DE), a university degree catalog, or a CEFR language skill landscape).

Only root curricula explicitly listed in curricula/curriculum_manifest.json are selectable in the UI and eligible for Champion registration:

{
  "curricula": [
    { "id": "a0e13c56-c25f-4742-9272-3a1a603ee52e", "title": "Gymnasium (DE)" }
  ]
}

Every manifest ID must exist under curricula/, must never point to a module or contained sub-landscape, and is verified by CI against the computed root set.

docs.title: 1.3. Level 2: Personal Curriculum
docs.text:
The Personal Curriculum is the learner's committed, durable scope inside the Base Curriculum — defining which authored curriculum view applies rather than temporary study focus. For German school curricula, the semantic selection order is:

  1. Jurisdiction (including an explicit canonical view where available);
  2. Duration model (such as G8 or G9 where relevant);
  3. Stage (lower secondary, upper secondary, or explicitly both);
  4. Selected subjects;
  5. Course profile per selected subject (where applicable).

Course profile is a per-subject attribute: Mathematics LK and Physics GK may coexist, LK never implies upper secondary, and missing stage data never silently defaults to cross-stage scope. Level 2 resolves the applicable composition view and bounds focus, frontier, progress, and completion; changing Level 2 revalidates focus and activeGoal without altering canonical goal IDs or erasing global mastery.

Single first-party editor contract: Level 2 is edited exclusively in SkillPilot's first-party WebGUI (on the start screen before launching a session and in the Cockpit afterward) over shared backend validation, normalization, and save rules. The OpenAI ChatClient neither presents nor mutates Level 2; if configuration is incomplete, it halts domain coaching and refers the learner back to the WebGUI.

docs.title: 1.4. Level 3: Learning Focus and Active Goal
docs.text:
Level 3 is intentionally lightweight and comprises two parts:

  • Level 3a — Focus: one or more scope roots selecting the active learning corridor (such as Grade 7, Q1, or Analysis; structural program units are not themselves canonical goals).
  • Level 3b — Active atomic goal: at most one concrete, assessable atomic goal serving as the immediate working target.

Focus widening follows the learner-facing ancestor path toward the root: the backend publishes valid broader ancestors that add unmastered target goals (nearest suitable ancestor first, preserving independent multi-root corridors in goalIds), and automatic widening is proposed only upon genuine completion of the current focus (never merely because the frontier is blocked), requiring learner confirmation.

Under the 4 November 2026 Assessment-Gated Completion clarification, requires alone never writes mastery to prerequisites; valid passed application assessments derive globally effective recognition of ordinary goals, so widening focus never reopens recognized competences.

docs.title: 1.5. Level 4: Mastery and the orthogonal timeline axis
docs.text:
Mastery is the learner's single durable outcome per stable atomic goal UUID — mastered or not mastered — remaining global across composition views and Level 2/3 changes without partial-mastery states. Effective mastery \(M_{\mathrm{eff}} = M \cup W\) combines stored explicit mastery \(M\) with assessment-gated recognition \(W\) (while assessment and memorization goals stay explicit; runtime migration remains pending, see 2.4). Cluster and scope percentages express the weighted share of effectively mastered atomic goals, never partial mastery of one goal.

Orthogonal curriculum timeline: A dated course or exam schedule is an execution-plan overlay answering when targets inside Level 2 should be addressed (see Unified Learning-Plan Status and Curriculum Time Axis and Pacing), not a fifth personalization level.

docs.title: 5. Portable Agent Runtime Architecture: Interchangeable MCP Hosts
docs.text:
Scope and Structure

Strategic architecture governing SkillPilot's long-term host and model-provider independence. Binding operational contracts for current coach adapters are specified in 6 through 10 and take precedence whenever details differ. Part A defines the durable normative architecture; Part B records the dated market assessment (as of 19 August 2026, complemented by subsequent repository decisions in 10).

docs.title: 5.1. Part A — Durable architecture: three-tier separation and core invariants
docs.text:
SkillPilot is structured long-term into three independently replaceable tiers:

  1. SkillPilot Core as the durable, provider-neutral learning system,
  2. an interchangeable AI Chat Application / MCP Host,
  3. an interchangeable Model Provider (preferably addressed via an Open-Responses-conformant interface).

Two Co-Equal Architectural Rules

  1. SkillPilot Core must depend neither on a specific chat host nor on a specific LLM provider.
  2. Per learner, SkillPilot Core persists exclusively structured, schema-validated learning and control state — never chat messages, learner phrasing, free-text answers, student work, images, attachments, or model grading transcripts.

Learning conversations do not vanish by keeping Core narrow: they reside in the MCP Host and (when vision is used) at the chosen Model Provider. Because no single platform today satisfies every requirement simultaneously (hosted runtime, cross-device chats, direct user-to-provider billing, Open Responses, Remote MCP, Skills, MCP Apps UI, Agent Plugins, mobile UX, voice dictation, vision, and minor-student eligibility), SkillPilot deliberately supports two operating tracks.

docs.title: Standards and their exact roles
docs.text: Standard / Term Normative role in SkillPilot Open Responses (vs. proprietary OpenAI Responses API or emulated /responses) Open specification between the Agent Runtime (MCP Host) and Model Provider/Gateway; conformance requires passing official acceptance tests plus SkillPilot's capability profile — never inferred from a /responses URL alone. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Standardizes connectivity between MCP Host/Client and SkillPilot Core as a Remote MCP Server over Streamable HTTP. MCP Apps Optional sandboxed HTML UI resources attached to MCP tools. Every SkillPilot tool supports plain-text output (universal fallback), structuredContent, and optional MCP Apps UI; no essential didactic step may depend solely on UI rendering. Agent Plugins v1 Portable install artifact (plugin.json, skills/.../SKILL.md, mcp.json); MCP Apps UIs are served live by the MCP server, and OAuth client profiles stay host-managed outside the plugin archive.

docs.title: Runtime and installation topology
docs.text:
End Devices (Mobile / Desktop Browser / App: Text, Dictation, Camera)
        | HTTPS
        v
AI Chat Application / MCP Host
  +-- Chat UI + Server-side Agent Runtime (Loop, Context, Attachments, MCP Client)
        |                                       |
        | Open Responses API / Gateway          | Remote MCP (Streamable HTTP + OAuth)
        v                                       v
Model Provider (Learner/Parent          SkillPilot Core
  account; vision images land HERE,       +-- MCP Server (Tools, Resources, MCP Apps UI)
  never inside SkillPilot Core)           +-- Didactic Services (Skill Graph, SRS, Exams)
                                          +-- Learning State DB (structured state only)

docs.title: 5.2. State boundaries, operating tracks, media, and billing
docs.text:
Processing domain Stored data Controller / owner MCP Host Chat user account, chat transcripts, messages, attachments, sessions, optional BYOK credentials Host operator (in self-hosted pilot: enpasos) Model Provider Submitted prompts and vision images under provider terms Model provider (direct contract with learner / parent) SkillPilot Core Structured learning and control state (learner link, curriculum/personalization, focus, activeGoal, binary mastery, SRS schedule, binary Verified Recall outcome) enpasos
  • No cross-host chat portability: Chat history is host-bound while learning state is SkillPilot-bound (learner, activeGoal, masteryValue, dueItems, lastRecallOutcome; nextRecommendedAction is computed dynamically rather than persisted). Active coach mutations exclude free-text fields (retiring legacy lastFeedback exceptions in active contracts; see 6.2).
  • Visible identifiers: A random, opaque learningSessionId is explicitly permitted inside model context, whereas internal learner, account, or database IDs remain strictly hidden.
  • Two durable operating tracks: Track A uses provider-hosted MCP hosts (ChatGPT, Claude) with near-zero infra overhead and direct consumer subscriptions; Track B uses a portable open-source MCP host (pilot: single-node Docker Compose LibreChat; secondary lab: Archestra) with BYOK, direct provider billing, and explicit operator policies for MongoDB backups, upload-volume retention, key rotation, and minor-protection access controls.
  • Dictation, ephemeral vision, and billing: Voice input converts to text in browser/host; photographed student work travels from MCP Host to the chosen vision Model Provider and never to SkillPilot Core (Core receives only structured writes such as setMastery with 1.0). Provider accounts and API credentials belong strictly to learners or parents/guardians — a central SkillPilot operator key reselling tokens is prohibited.

docs.title: 5.3. Phased roadmap and mandatory host acceptance suite
docs.text:
1. Phase 1 — Stabilize interfaces: Host-neutral Remote MCP surface (Streamable HTTP, OAuth 2.0, stable tool names, versioned schemas, idempotency, text fallback, structuredContent, optional MCP Apps) plus canonical Agent Plugin bundle with zero image/solution upload tools.
  2. Phase 2 & 3 — Self-hosted pilot & standards lab: Closed LibreChat pilot (5–10 testers across phone/desktop, dictation, vision, BYOK) alongside practical evaluation of Archestra (Open Responses acceptance tests, MCP Apps).
  3. Phase 4 & 5 — Hosted channels & future managed host: Claude (adult testers) and ChatGPT (directory release) sharing the same SkillPilot Core state; migration to a third-party managed portable host only once all 12 requirements (Open Responses, BYOK, MCP Apps, Agent Plugins, export/deletion, minor-eligible accounts) are proven.

Mandatory host and model acceptance gates: Cross-device session continuation without conflicting writes; 60 s German domain dictation triggering a tool call; phone-camera handwritten solution analysis with documented vision-provider retention; MCP negative test (proving zero image bytes, OCR text, solution prose, image URLs, or grading transcripts in MCP args, logs, traces, or DB); credential negative test; mobile OAuth refresh and opaque learningSessionId with zero internal ID leaks; write idempotency; account/chat deletion verification; complete text-only learning flow plus sandboxed MCP Apps check; direct user billing; official Open Responses test suite.

docs.title: 5. Architekturkonzept: SkillPilot mit austauschbarem MCP Host
docs.text:
Geltungsbereich und Aufbau

Strategiekonzept für die langfristige Host- und Anbieterunabhängigkeit von SkillPilot. Die verbindlichen Laufzeitverträge des ausgelieferten Coach-Pfades stehen in 6 bis 10; bei Abweichungen gelten jene Verträge. Teil A definiert die stabile, normative Zielarchitektur; Teil B dokumentiert den datierten Marktanhang (Stand 19. August 2026, ergänzt um die nachfolgenden Repo-Entscheidungen aus 10).

docs.title: 5.1. Teil A — Stabile Architektur: Drei-Ebenen-Trennung und Kerngrenzen
docs.text:
SkillPilot besteht langfristig aus drei unabhängig austauschbaren Bereichen:

  1. SkillPilot Core als dauerhaftes, anbieterneutrales Lernsystem,
  2. einer austauschbaren AI Chat Application bzw. einem MCP Host,
  3. einem austauschbaren Model Provider (bevorzugt über eine Open-Responses-kompatible Schnittstelle).

Zwei gleichrangige Architekturregeln

  1. SkillPilot Core darf weder von einem bestimmten Chat-Host noch von einem bestimmten LLM-Anbieter abhängig sein.
  2. SkillPilot Core persistiert pro Lernendem ausschließlich strukturierten, schema-validierten Lern- und Steuerungszustand — keinerlei Chatnachrichten, Formulierungen, Freitextantworten, Schülerlösungen, Bilder, Anhänge oder modellseitige Analyseprotokolle.

Die Lernkommunikation verschwindet dadurch nicht: Sie liegt beim MCP Host und (bei Vision-Nutzung) beim gewählten Model Provider. Weil heute kein einzelner Dienst alle Anforderungen gleichzeitig erfüllt (gehostete Agent Runtime, geräteübergreifende Chats, direkte Nutzer-Provider-Abrechnung, Open Responses, Remote MCP, Skills, MCP Apps UI, Agent Plugins, Mobile, Sprache, Vision und Minderjährigeneignung), verfolgt SkillPilot bewusst zwei Betriebswege parallel.

docs.title: Standards und ihre Rollen
docs.text: Standard / Begriff Verbindliche Rolle in SkillPilot Open Responses (vs. proprietäre OpenAI Responses API oder nachgebildetes /responses) Offene Spezifikation zwischen Agent Runtime (MCP Host) und Model Provider/Gateway; Konformität zählt nur per Acceptance-Test und Capability-Profil, niemals bloß wegen des Pfadnamens /responses. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Standardisiert die Verbindung zwischen MCP Host/Client und SkillPilot Core als Remote-MCP-Server über Streamable HTTP. MCP Apps Optionale interaktive HTML-Ressourcen in Host-Sandboxen. Jedes SkillPilot-Tool unterstützt Textausgabe (universeller Fallback), structuredContent und optionale MCP-Apps-UI; keine didaktische Pflichtaktion darf ausschließlich per UI möglich sein. Agent Plugins v1 Portables Installationsartefakt (plugin.json, skills/.../SKILL.md, mcp.json); MCP-Apps-UIs kommen zur Laufzeit vom MCP-Server, und OAuth-Client-Profile bleiben hostverwaltet außerhalb des Plugins.

        v                                       v

  nicht im SkillPilot Core)              +-- Didactic Services (Skill-Graph, SRS, Exams)

docs.title: 5.2. Zustandsgrenzen, Betriebswege, Medien und Abrechnung
docs.text:
Bereich Gespeicherte Daten Verantwortlich MCP Host Benutzerkonto, Chatverläufe, Nachrichten, Anhänge, Sitzungen, ggf. BYOK-Credentials Hostbetreiber (im eigenen Pilot: enpasos) Model Provider Übermittelte Prompts und Vision-Bilddaten gemäß Anbieterbedingungen Modellanbieter (direkter Vertrag mit Lernendem / Eltern) SkillPilot Core Strukturierter Lern- und Steuerungszustand (Zuordnung, Curriculum/Personalisierung, Fokus, activeGoal, binäre Mastery, SRS-Planung, binäres Verified-Recall-Ergebnis) enpasos
  • Keine hostübergreifende Chatportabilität: Der Chatverlauf ist hostgebunden, der Lernzustand SkillPilot-gebunden (learner, activeGoal, masteryValue, dueItems, lastRecallOutcome; nextRecommendedAction wird abgeleitet statt frei persistiert). Aktive Coach-Mutationen sind frei von Freitextfeldern (historische lastFeedback-Altlasten werden im aktiven Vertrag ausgeschlossen; siehe 6.2).
  • Sichtbare Kennungen: Eine zufällige, opake learningSessionId ist im Modellkontext ausdrücklich erlaubt; permanente Lernenden-, Konto- oder Datenbank-IDs bleiben strikt verborgen.
  • Zwei dauerhafte Betriebswege: Betriebsweg A nutzt fremdbetriebene Plattform-Hosts (ChatGPT, Claude) mit minimalem Eigenbetrieb und direktem Consumer-Abo; Betriebsweg B nutzt einen portablen Open-Source-MCP-Host (Pilot: LibreChat per Docker Compose; Zweitkandidat: Archestra) mit BYOK, direkter Providerabrechnung und kontrollierbarer Datenhaltung (inkl. dokumentierter Backup-, Upload-Lösch-, Key-Rotations- und Zugriffsregeln).
  • Sprache, flüchtige Bildanalyse und Abrechnung: Diktat wird im Browser/Host zu Text gewandelt; fotografierte Lösungen gehen vom Host an das Vision-Modell des gewählten Providers und niemals an SkillPilot Core (Core erhält nur den strukturierten Schreibaufruf wie setMastery mit 1.0). Providerkonto und Modell-Credentials gehören stets Lernenden bzw. Erziehungsberechtigten — ein zentraler SkillPilot-Betreiber-Key mit Weiterberechnung ist ausgeschlossen.

docs.title: 5.3. Stufenplan und verbindliche Host-Abnahmetests
docs.text:
1. Phase 1 — Schnittstellen stabilisieren: Hostunabhängiger Remote-MCP-Vertrag (Streamable HTTP, OAuth 2.0, stabile Toolnamen, versionierte Schemas, Idempotenz, Text-Fallback, structuredContent, optionale MCP Apps) plus kanonisches Agent-Plugin-Paket ohne Upload-Tools für Bilder/Lösungen.
  2. Phase 2 & 3 — Selbst betriebener Pilot & Standardslabor: Kleiner geschlossener LibreChat-Pilot (5–10 Tester, Smartphone/Desktop, Diktat, Vision, BYOK) parallel zur praktischen Erprobung von Archestra (Open-Responses-Tests, MCP Apps).
  3. Phase 4 & 5 — Hosted Channels & künftiger Managed Host: Claude (volljährige Tester) und ChatGPT (Verzeichnis-Release) auf demselben SkillPilot-Lernzustand; späterer Wechsel auf einen fremdbetriebenen portablen Host erst bei Nachweis aller 12 Kriterien (inkl. Open Responses, BYOK, MCP Apps, Agent Plugins, Datenexport/Löschung und Jugendschutz).

Pflicht-Abnahmetests für jeden Host und jedes Modell: Geräteübergreifende Sitzungsfortsetzung ohne Race-Conditions; 60 s deutsches Fachdiktat mit Tool-Call; Smartphone-Kamerafoto mit dokumentiertem Vision-Providerpfad; MCP-Negativtest (weder Bilddaten, OCR, Lösungstext, Bild-URL noch Analyseprotokoll in MCP-Argumenten, Logs, Traces oder DB); Credential-Negativtest; OAuth-Refresh und opake learningSessionId ohne interne ID-Lecks; Schreib-Idempotenz; Konto-/Chat-Löschtest; vollständiger Ablauf ohne MCP Apps sowie Sandbox-Prüfung mit MCP Apps; direkte Nutzerabrechnung; offizielle Open-Responses-Tests.

docs.title: Curriculum Time Axis, Buffer Planning, and Target-vs-Actual Learning Pace
docs.text:
Status: Target concept; local, purely browser-based planning pilot implemented. The backend-authoritative target architecture is still open.

Binding correction of 21 September 2026: Stored learning-goal results are the sole source of goal achievement in the Cockpit, learning-goal tree, and teacher planning. The former manual instructional progress state (CoverageEvent, CoverageLedgerAttestation, instructional actuals together with their associated curve, forecast, and confirmation workflow) is superseded, including as a future target architecture. The corresponding technical design details in Sections 4–18 and in the historical staged rollout plan remain preserved to contextualize existing datasets; they are not active implementation or acceptance requirements. Legacy data is neither deleted nor reinterpreted as mastery. The current pilot contract is defined in Section 19.1; personal target-vs-actual status is governed by the Unified Learning-Plan Status Concept.

Outcome boundary of 29 October 2026: Mastery is the sole stored outcome state per learning goal: achieved or still open. This also applies to exam goals. Planning reads this state and may evaluate event timestamps for trajectory metrics; it introduces no separate pass projection, no qualifying secondary proof, and no stored failed attempts. The former requirement for AssessmentResultEvent is withdrawn. Missing timestamp or reporting data limits the evaluable history, not the recognition of existing mastery. Percentage values aggregate across multiple goals.

Scope: First-party SkillPilot WebGUI and backend; no implicit modification of published provider contracts or historical artifacts.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
SkillPilot should answer not only what is to be learned and what is already mastered, but also:

  • when a subject section is scheduled to start and end,
  • how much real instructional capacity is available during that period,
  • how much buffer remains deliberately protected,
  • what progress is expected by a given date,
  • which concrete learning or exam goals should be completed by a milestone date,
  • how quickly new learning goals have actually been achieved since the individual learning start,
  • whether the stored individual learning progress matches the plan,
  • how a teacher can present both the plan and the current plan posture transparently on a single page to department heads or school leadership,
  • and what transparent plan adjustment would make sense when deviations occur.

The primary school scenario is a subject course planned by a teacher. The same model must also work for a personal learning plan without a class. The school leadership view is an access-controlled projection of the very same course plan, aggregated by default, rather than a separate reporting system with diverging numbers.

docs.title: 2. Core Decision
docs.text:
From a user perspective, a cluster such as "Linear Functions" sits on the time axis as a bar with a concrete start-to-end date range. Technically, however, the canonical cluster receives no date fields.

The time axis is a dedicated, versioned planning layer:

  • Goals and clusters define what is learned.
  • programUnits and goalPlacements define where a goal resides within a program.
  • The Composition View defines which unambiguous tree a resolved scope sees.
  • A curriculum pacing plan defines when and with what capacity a class or individual works through this material.
  • Mastery defines what an individual has mastered based on available evidence.

Absolute dates belong neither on canonical clusters nor on programUnits, goalPlacements, or Composition Views. The same cluster can fall into different time windows across different classes, school years, federal states, and individual plans.

The pacing plan is therefore an execution schedule orthogonal to the four personalization levels. It is neither a new learning goal nor a replacement for Personal Curriculum, focus, frontier, or mastery.

flowchart LR
    C[Curriculum and Composition View] --> R[Resolved target atomic goals]
    R --> P[Versioned curriculum pacing plan]
    K[Instructional calendar and capacity] --> P
    P --> S[Planned curve]
    M[Stored learning-goal results] --> A[Individual goal achievement]
    S --> V[Target vs. actual, forecast, and buffer]
    A --> V

docs.title: 3. Single Outcome State, Explicitly Named Planning Scope
docs.text:
Teachers and learners see the same stored results per learner:

  1. Planned target: What should have been achieved by today according to the pacing plan?
  2. Goal achievement: Which goals have been achieved according to the stored learning state?

A plan determines dates and scope, not learning outcomes. There is no additional manual instructional confirmation that reveals or hides a stored completion. A completed orientation goal likewise counts within its goal scope without thereby proving subject-matter mastery.

The full personal goal scope may be larger than the plan set G recorded at the start of the plan—for example due to previously achieved goals or a narrower planning scope. Wherever scopes match, the exact same counting rules apply everywhere; differing scopes are named explicitly. An unchanged planning baseline is not a current learning state. Querying progress rewrites neither the plan nor stored results.

Missing or stale results remain recognizable as unavailable rather than producing an apparently reliable zero balance. Former coverage documentation is not used as a fallback source.

docs.title: 4.1 InstructionalCalendar — Instructional Calendar
docs.text:
The calendar describes the time available specifically for a given course or personal plan:

  • school year and IANA time zone, for example Europe/Berlin,
  • recurring subject lessons with their duration in minutes,
  • school holidays, public holidays, and weeks without subject instruction,
  • cancellations, class trips, project days, and other exclusions,
  • additional or rescheduled lessons.

Internally, minutes should serve as the shared capacity unit. The UI can render them as lesson periods, double periods, or clock hours. This keeps 45-, 60-, and 90-minute lesson models comparable.

Calendar data is plan-local or reusable at the institutional level. It does not belong inside a curriculum package because holidays and timetables depend on the school year, location, school, class, and subject.

The calendar provides only available subject capacity. How that capacity is allocated to initial instruction, review, assessment, remediation, buffer, or still-unallocated time belongs exclusively in the pacing plan. This ensures the same minute is never deducted in the calendar and then booked a second time in the plan.

docs.title: 4.2 PacingPlan — Curriculum Pacing Plan
docs.text:
A pacing plan is a stably identified plan for a class or an individual learner. It contains at least:

  • owner type class or learner,
  • title, subject, and school year,
  • the complete Level 2 fingerprint as its validity context,
  • an explicit planningScope, for example subject plus grade level, program unit, or Composition subtree,
  • references to Curriculum, Composition View, and Instructional Calendar,
  • scheduleStartDate and the final plan end date of the shared time grid,
  • a versioned interpretation of the existing mastery state; mastery-threshold-0.9-v1 denotes solely the legacy numeric compatibility evaluation, not a graded subject-matter mastery scale,
  • status draft, published, or retired,
  • a sequence of immutable revisions.

A class plan represents the shared target schedule. A PlanAssignment binds a learner to the plan through time-bounded revision bindings and records that learner's learning start and baseline. A personal plan can exist without a class plan.

docs.title: 4.3 PlanRevision — Immutable Published Revision
docs.text:
Drafts may be edited. A published revision is never overwritten. It stores:

  • revision number and effectiveFrom,
  • predecessor revision and reason for change,
  • scope and projection digests,
  • immutable calendar revision and calendar digest,
  • materialized daily or weekly capacity including all exclusions and overrides,
  • the goal set resolved at that time,
  • positive reference capacity referenceWeekMinutes and start-of-week day,
  • timeline blocks, milestones, pins, and buffers,
  • a versioned calculation and display policy for measurement windows, minimum observation thresholds, and speedometer scaling,
  • creator and creation timestamp,
  • a version number for optimistic locking.

When replanning, the past portion of the effective schedule is preserved. Only the future portion is replaced by a new revision. Historical target-vs-actual reports therefore cannot be retroactively "planned into the green." Every revision has a half-open validity interval. Plan-local units of already bound goals remain constant across successor revisions; the new planned curve starts with the unchanged continuity offset of the previous curve. Without a new mastery or coverage event, switching revisions must not create a jump in target, actual, or variance values.

docs.title: 4.4 TimelineBlock — Timeline Block
docs.text:
A timeline block is the visible bar on the time axis. It contains:

  • a stable block ID and a human-readable label,
  • an explicit reference to a canonical cluster or a stable Composition View node,
  • startDate and endDateInclusive as local calendar dates,
  • a role,
  • scheduledGoalIds as the materialized set of all goals worked on in this block,
  • countedTargetGoalIds as the unambiguous subset that counts toward planned progress for the first time in this block,
  • separate digests for both goal sets,
  • explicitly allocated minutes or lesson slots and their distribution within the date range,
  • when bound to milestones, stable capacity slices with ID, source slot, minute share, and exactly one workItemGoalId prepared by that slice,
  • plan-local planning units and optional goal overrides,
  • optional pins on start dates, end dates, or milestones,
  • the forecast horizon d_b materialized at publication time, derived from the earliest binding pin of this block or its own end date.

Recommended roles for the initial contract:

  • primary: initial scheduled instruction; counts toward planned progress,
  • revisit: review; consumes capacity, does not count goals a second time,
  • assessment: exam or diagnostic check; consumes capacity, provides an assessment slot, and can be linked to a milestone, but is itself neither a milestone nor silent proof of mastery,
  • remediation: explicit catch-up work on prerequisites or gaps,
  • buffer: protected reserve without learning-goal points.

A block may reference a structural node, but its scheduled goal set is deterministically compiled upon publication. Historical evaluations do not re-expand the reference against a subsequently modified live tree.

A date range alone does not yet reserve capacity. For every block, it must therefore be specified which minutes or concrete subject slots it occupies. A simple initial variant distributes allocatedMinutes proportionally across the slots available within the block's date range; explicit slot assignments override this distribution. Only this makes both the planned curve and overbooking checks deterministic. A capacity slice remains owned by exactly one block; milestones merely reference it and do not create a second time booking. If an instructional phase combines multiple goals, planning splits its minutes conservatively across multiple slices. That is a planning approximation, not a claim about second-by-second classroom impact.

The sum of work slices must not exceed the content minutes of the block. Block minutes not broken down further remain visible for coarse block planning, but must not inflate the denominator of a milestone speedometer.

Accordingly, a buffer block materializes BufferCapacitySlice entries with ID, source slot, and minute share, but without a learning goal. Referencing a buffer in a forecast does not release that buffer yet; only a new effective revision may turn it into content capacity.

Within a revision, each buffer slice carries at most one forecastReservationKey. This reserves it exclusively for exactly one still-open forecast commitment—either a block or a milestone. Multiple displays may reference the same reservation only if they describe the exact same functional workload according to goal-set and occurrence digests; even then, the capacity is counted only once across the course. A functionally different block, milestone, or second forecast must not claim the same buffer slice again as reserve.

In the first version, programUnits may group rows or headings on the time axis, but they are not a valid block target: a program unit does not possess an unambiguous atomic goal set of its own. A later extension would require a dedicated, scope-bound expansion rule via goalPlacements.

docs.title: 4.5 PlanMilestone — Concrete Goals by a Target Date
docs.text:
In addition to longer cluster blocks, a plan can contain a due-date-sorted list of concrete milestones, for example:

Abitur Mathematics problems by 15 March 2027

A milestone contains:

  • stable ID, clear title, and dueDate,
  • functional kind kind: learning | assessment | exam,
  • deadline bindingness deadlinePolicy: target | hard,
  • workloadGoalIds: the concrete learning goals that may be scheduled as the functionally admissible preparation workload for this milestone,
  • when referencing a cluster, the materialized goal set including its digest,
  • exactly one typed fulfillment rule: allCurrentlyMastered(goalIds), atLeastNCurrentlyMastered(goalIds, n); for exam milestones, these rules reference the exam learning goals,
  • the functional references of the fulfillment rule kept separate from the preparation workload,
  • concrete capacityAllocationIds pointing to capacity slices with exactly one goal ID and a minute share,
  • optional releasableBufferAllocationIds that fall no later than the local due date and are designated as releasable buffer specifically for this forecast,
  • as well as the designated assessment slot where applicable.

This separation is essential: in the example "Abitur Mathematics problems by 15 March 2027", the preparatory learning goals can govern gradual progress and required pace, whereas mastery of the concrete exam learning goals governs completion of the milestone.

The initial contract deliberately restricts admissible combinations:

  • kind: learning uses a mastery-based rule; in the initial contract, its set of admissible goal IDs is identical to workloadGoalIds.
  • kind: assessment | exam uses allCurrentlyMastered across the exam learning goals. Their IDs are functionally linked to the preparation workload via a published assessmentGoalMapping. The preparation workload may be empty, in which case no pace speedometer exists.

For the first pacing-plan version, assessmentId is the stable canonical ID of the exam/assessment goal. A content digest of its approved examData, including the grading rubric, describes the scheduled task and its authoring revision. It is not an additional individual success condition: existing mastery of this stable goal ID counts immediately. A functionally different learning goal requires an appropriately reviewed goal model, not a hidden second pass status attached to the existing goal ID.

For atLeastNCurrentlyMastered, each PlanAssignment additionally materializes activeWorkloadGoalIds before rendering a speedometer. First, all alternatives currently mastered with rule effect are taken into account—both baseline goals and goals achieved after learning start, even if they were not previously selected. If their count is already at least n, the rule is fulfilled and there is no remaining open speedometer workload. Otherwise, the assignment adds exactly n - q concrete still-open alternatives, where q is the number of these currently rule-effective completions.

A relevant mastery event therefore triggers a deterministic, logged rematerialization: existing still-open selections are retained in stable selection order, with only surplus trailing entries dropped or missing slots explicitly filled. Thus, newly mastering a previously unselected alternative goal immediately reduces the open workload accurately. As long as the required open selection has not been determined, the UI displays the alternatives group rather than a single pseudo-precise pointer. Changing the selection freely is an audited assignment adjustment; the broader set of functionally admissible alternatives remains unchanged and visible.

target denotes an adjustable target date. hard denotes an external or deliberately fixed date that neither tolerance bands nor automatic replanning may shift. Modifying it requires a new revision, the appropriate capability, and both actor and rationale; for a class plan, this is normally the authorized teacher, and for a personal plan, its owner. Externally mandated exam dates may only be superseded by an equally authorized replacement date.

Milestones can originate from the published class plan or be added personally. A personal entry modifies neither the class plan nor other learners' milestones and must remain resolvable within the learner's own Personal Curriculum.

The milestone itself consumes no minutes and generates no mastery. The associated primary, revisit, assessment, or remediation blocks carry the capacity. A fixed milestone can pin those blocks' end dates and forms a boundary for forecasting and replanning.

For pace calculations, only the content capacity explicitly allocated to this preparation workload up to the end of the local dueDate counts. An underlying slot allocation may serve multiple milestones as the same work if it prepares the exact same workItemGoalId there via the same capacity slice; this avoids double-booking any minute in the overall plan. By contrast, two functionally disjoint milestone workloads must not each claim the same capacity share for themselves. Where workloads overlap only partially, solely the slices belonging to the genuinely shared goal IDs may be referenced multiple times. Required prerequisites and assessment slots must likewise fall no later than the due date. For buffer slices, the shared revision-wide exclusivity rule from Section 4.4 applies. Once buffer is actually released, the new revision regenerates subsequent forecasts from the remaining reserve.

All fulfillment rules read the current mastery state. If mastery is legitimately revoked or corrected on subject-matter grounds, a previously fulfilled milestone can become open again. A later ordinary failed attempt on an exam does not revoke existing mastery. No pass projection exists independently of mastery.

Fulfillment status is evaluated per PlanAssignment. A class milestone is therefore not summarily "done for the class" merely because a single learner has fulfilled it; course coverage remains a separate track.

For each fulfillment rule, the projection materializes its chronologically ordered validity episodes—that is, every transition into and out of "rule currently fulfilled." Before the due date, it distinguishes openBeforeDue and currentlyFulfilledBeforeDue; after the due date, completedOnTime, completedLate, overdueOpen, and currentlyReopened. Decisive are the end of the local due date in the plan revision's time zone and calendar, the truth value of the rule at that exact boundary, and the current episode:

  • If the rule is fulfilled today and was fulfilled at the end of the due date, the status is completedOnTime.
  • If it is fulfilled today, but was open at the end of the due date, the status is completedLate; the UI shows the start of the current re-fulfillment episode, not some earlier historical completion.
  • If it is open today and there has never been a valid fulfillment episode, the status is overdueOpen.
  • If it is open today and there was at least one prior valid fulfillment episode, the status is currentlyReopened; the metadata fields fulfilledAtDue and reopenedAt additionally preserve whether the rule held at the end of the due date and when the most recent episode reopened.

An initial completion before the due date therefore does not retroactively make a later re-fulfillment on time if the rule was open on the due date itself. Conversely, losing mastery only after the due date does not erase the historically accurate statement that the milestone was fulfilled on the due date. Append-only correction chains can transparently re-evaluate the episode projection for a new snapshot; the old snapshot remains stable via its watermark.

From the plan revision and milestones, the runtime first compiles sorted DatedGoalOccurrenceTemplate entries for the concrete goal list. Each entry has a stable occurrence key, a functional goal or assessment ID, a role, a date, exactly one date source, and an explicit dateSemantics:

  • deadline applies only to a published milestone, an explicitly ordered or dated goal occurrence, or a concrete assessment slot;
  • contextEnd is purely a display fallback to the end of its own primary, revisit, or remediation block.

A contextEnd merely states "this goal lies within this time segment." It is not an independent target deadline and must never trigger overdue, completedLate, or an atomic target quota. The user interface labels the date semantics explicitly rather than making both kinds of dates look identical. As a result, the same goal may carry multiple visible dates—such as "learn," "review," and "assess"—while still counting only once toward primary planning units. A minimum-count requirement is rendered as an "at least n of m" group with genuine alternatives rather than decomposed into m seemingly mandatory individual goals.

Per assignment, DatedGoalOccurrenceStatus projects orthogonal fields rather than overlapping single status values:

  • completionState: open | done,
  • scheduleState: noDeadline | notDue | overdue | completedOnTime | completedLate,
  • readinessState: ready | blocked including blockedReasons,
  • data quality of the information available for the report.

For a compact primary badge, precedence is deterministically done before overdue before blocked before open; the remaining fields stay visible alongside it. A goal that is both open past a genuine deadline and functionally blocked is therefore labeled primarily "overdue" while additionally explaining its blockers. A currently mastered goal remains "done" even if a prerequisite gap is surfaced separately. contextEnd always enforces scheduleState: noDeadline.

For primary learning goals, completion and readiness follow from current mastery and effective prerequisites. For review or remediation, a dedicated PlanActivityEvent is required; existing mastery and mere course coverage do not prove this personal activity. For assessments, the learning-goal outcome likewise follows exclusively from mastery. Initial exam dates and retake dates remain scheduling dates, not separate outcome states. From mastery alone, neither the attended exam sitting nor any failed attempt can be reconstructed; any corresponding historical statement remains unknown without reliable process data.

Free-form checklist items without a stable functional reference are possible as organizational notes, but count neither toward the planned curve nor as achieved learning goals. "Task opened" or "covered in class" does not automatically fulfill a functional milestone; its published fulfillment rule remains decisive.

docs.title: 4.6 PlanAssignment — Assignment and Learning Start
docs.text:
The assignment linking a plan lineage and a learner maintains a sequence of effective AssignmentRevisionBinding entries and additionally records:

  • assignedAt and the functional learningStartedAt,
  • the goal IDs already mastered at start as the baseline,
  • the baseline digest and baseline planning units,
  • the comparison mode classSchedule or rebaseAtStart,
  • assignment-specific active goal selections for alternative milestones,
  • optional authorized individual calendar adjustments,
  • assignment status and end timestamp.

Learning start is not automatically account creation, first login, or first mastery update. When a learner joins a class late, personal velocity measurement begins at actual entry.

classSchedule continues to compare a late entrant against the published class schedule. rebaseAtStart, by contrast, distributes only the personal goal workload remaining after the baseline starting from the individual learning start. The mode is chosen explicitly rather than inferred from data.

In classSchedule mode, individual absences alter personal remaining capacity and forecasts, not retroactively the shared class planned curve.
